guide_sections.heading: What each accessor returns from the starter record
guide_sections.body:
All rows below use the starter `record` with fields id, values and metadata.

```text
expression                       class      result
record["values"]                 list       one-element list named values
record[["values"]]               numeric    2 4
record$values                    numeric    2 4
record[["metadata"]][["unit"]]   character  "kg"
record[["missing"]]              NULL       NULL
record$val                       numeric    2 4
record[["val"]]                  NULL       NULL
```

The last two rows explain the advice to use `[[` with an exact name. The dollar operator does partial matching on lists, so a truncated name like `val` quietly finds `values`. Double brackets require the full name and return NULL, which a later `is.numeric()` check rejects. A missing field also returns NULL rather than an error, so checking `names(record)` first gives a clearer failure than discovering a NULL several steps later.

exercises.approach: Apply single brackets to the list and test the class of the result.
exercises.why: Single brackets select a sub-list. `record[1]` is a list holding one element named id, not the string "A" itself.
exercises.wrong: Expecting the contained value, as `record[[1]]` would return. Code that then calls `nchar()` or `toupper()` on the result gets a list method or an error instead of text handling.

exercises.approach: Extract in two stages: `record[["values"]]` gives the numeric vector, then `[[1]]` gives its first element.
exercises.why: The values field holds 2 and 4, so the first number is 2. Each stage has one clear job.
exercises.wrong: Writing `record["values"][[1]]`. The first step keeps the list wrapper, so `[[1]]` unwraps it and returns the whole vector 2, 4 instead of a single number.
exercises.verify: The reference check `record[["values"]][[1]] == 2` passes and the result has length 1.

exercises.approach: Check that both names exist, then check that id is one character string and values is numeric.
exercises.why: Testing names first makes a missing field fail with a clear message. The type checks then confirm the starter's id "A" is a single string and values 2, 4 are numbers.
exercises.wrong: Only testing `!is.null(record$id)`. That passes for an id of 7 or of c("A", "B"), neither of which identifies one record.
exercises.verify: On the starter record every check passes; setting `record$id <- 7` makes the stopifnot report `is.character(record$id) is not TRUE`.

exercises.approach: Replace the single-bracket argument with `record[["values"]]` so mean receives the numeric vector.
exercises.why: `record["values"]` is a list containing the vector. mean does not look inside lists, so it cannot average 2 and 4 from it.
exercises.wrong: Calling `mean(record["values"])`. It returns NA with a warning that the argument is not numeric or logical, and a script that ignores warnings carries the NA forward.

exercises.approach: Assign a list containing NULL through single brackets: `record["note"] <- list(NULL)`.
exercises.why: Single-bracket replacement sets list elements from the list on the right, so the note element is created and holds NULL. The record now has three fields.
exercises.wrong: Writing `record$note <- NULL`. Assigning NULL with the dollar or double-bracket form removes a field; here note does not exist yet, so nothing is added at all.
exercises.verify: `"note" %in% names(record)` returns TRUE, `is.null(record$note)` is TRUE, and `length(record)` returns 3.

exercises.approach: Keep mixed records as lists and extract each field with its own type; flatten only fields that share one type.
exercises.why: The id is text and values are numbers. `unlist()` needs a common type, so it converts everything to character, as Example 3 shows.
exercises.wrong: Flattening and then calling `as.numeric()` to recover the numbers. The id becomes NA with a coercion warning, so one field is destroyed to repair another.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `is.character(unlist(record[c("id", "values")]))`, and the flattened result has length 3 from two fields.

run_note: The starter builds one record with a scalar `id`, a numeric `values` vector and a nested `metadata` list holding the unit kg, then shows it with `str()`. Run it and read the indentation: `str()` marks `metadata` as a list inside the list, the structure that `unlist()` would flatten away. Every extraction you write should state whether it returns a sublist, as single brackets do, or the element itself, as double brackets and `$` do. The printed `str()` output after each step is how you confirm which one you actually received.
checks_note: The assertions confirm that `record[1]` is still a list while `record[["values"]][[1]]` is the number 2, that `id` and `values` are present with the right types and `id` has length one, that the mean of `values` is 3, that a missing `note` field reads as NULL, and that `unlist()` on `id` and `values` coerces everything to character. They do not validate deeper nesting or fields added later.
